addmaths-0606-int-reverse.description: Find a family of curves from a gradient function and select the one that passes through a stated point.

sections.title: What is being reversed?
sections.label: Inverse process

blocks.html:
Integration reverses differentiation by finding functions with the specified derivative.

If \(F'(x)=f(x)\), then \(\int f(x)\,\mathrm dx=F(x)+C\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Check the antiderivative by differentiating back to the integrand.

Look at one term at a time. For \(f(x)=6x-4\), the first term comes from \(3x^2\), since differentiating it brings down a factor of two. The constant term comes from \(-4x\).

Write \(3x^2-4x+C\) and differentiate it. Both variable terms must match the given gradient.

blocks.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient
blocks.prompt:
A curve has gradient function \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=18 x^{2} - 2\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: An antiderivative gives a family. Use the point only after writing the family.
blocks.solution:
Find a function whose derivative is the stated gradient. Add the unknown constant.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(18 x^{2} - 2\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 6 x^{3} - 2 x\).

retry.feedback: Differentiate the variable terms in the proposed expression. The arbitrary constant disappears, but a different coefficient changes the gradient.

blocks.html: A derivative alone does not determine the constant value.

blocks.title: Find the coefficient from its derivative
blocks.prompt: The curve \(y=ax^3-3x+C\) has gradient \(12x^2-3\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: The derivative of \(ax^3\) is \(3ax^2\). Match this to \(12x^2\).
blocks.solution: Comparing the two coefficients gives \(3a=12\), so \(a=4\).

retry.feedback: Differentiating \(ax^3\) multiplies its coefficient by three. Divide \(12\) by three.

sections.intro: Start with a derivative and ask which original function would give it. For a term such as \(6x\), test \(3x^2\) by differentiating.

sections.title: Why is there an arbitrary constant?
sections.label: Arbitrary constant

blocks.html:
Adding any constant makes a vertical translation whose derivative is unchanged.

\(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}[F(x)+C]=F'(x)\) for every constant \(C\).

figure.alt: The two parabolas have parallel tangents at x = 1.
figure.caption: The lower curve is \(y=x^2-1\) and the upper curve is \(y=x^2+3\). At \(x=1\) their heights differ by four, but both tangents have gradient two.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Write the general antiderivative with the arbitrary constant before substituting a condition.

Compare two curves at the same x-coordinate. Their difference \((F(x)+C_2)-(F(x)+C_1)=C_2-C_1\) is the same throughout the common interval.

blocks.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient
blocks.prompt:
A curve has gradient function \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\). Use \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: An antiderivative gives a family. Use the point only after writing the family.
blocks.solution:
Find a function whose derivative is the stated gradient. Add the unknown constant.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(4 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 4 \sqrt{x} + 4 x\).

retry.feedback: Differentiate the variable terms in the proposed expression. The arbitrary constant disappears, but a different coefficient changes the gradient.

blocks.html: Omitting the constant loses all but one of the possible curves.

blocks.title: Compare two heights with the same gradient
blocks.prompt: Two curves have gradient function \(2x\). At \(x=1\) their heights are \(-3\) and \(2\). Find their vertical separation at \(x=5\).
blocks.hint: Both curves have the form \(x^2+C\). Their difference is independent of \(x\).
blocks.solution: The separation at \(x=1\) is \(2-(-3)=5\). The same vertical shift holds for every \(x\), including \(5\).

sections.intro: Every vertical shift of a curve gives the same gradient. Write one arbitrary constant to represent all those shifts.

sections.title: How does a point select one curve?
sections.label: Particular curve

blocks.html:
A point gives an input and output for the antiderivative.

If \(y=F(x)+C\) passes through \((a,b)\), then \(C=b-F(a)\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Substitute both coordinates, solve for the constant and then evaluate the particular function.

Use the known x-coordinate inside the variable part first. Subtract that value from the known y-coordinate. Substitute the resulting \(C\) back into the whole equation before predicting another height.

blocks.title: Your turn
blocks.prompt: A curve has gradient \(6x-2\) and passes through \((1,7)\). Find \(y\) when \(x=0\).
blocks.hint: After integrating, use the given point to find \(C\). Then put \(x=0\) in the curve equation.
blocks.solution: The general equation is \(y=3x^2-2x+C\). At \(x=1\), \(7=1+C\), so \(C=6\) and \(y(0)=6\).

retry.feedback: The given point fixes \(C\). The variable part has value \(1\) at \(x=1\), but \(y(1)=7\).

blocks.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient

Answer: \(C - 7 x + \frac{7}{x}\).

retry.feedback: Differentiate the variable terms in the proposed expression. The arbitrary constant disappears, but a different coefficient changes the gradient.

blocks.html: The gradient at a point is different from the point's y-coordinate.

blocks.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient
blocks.prompt:

Find the constant of integration for the curve through \((1,9)\).
blocks.hint: An antiderivative gives a family. Use the point only after writing the family.
blocks.solution:
Write the curve as \(y=C + 8 x + \frac{1}{x}\). Substituting the coordinates gives \(9=9+C\).

Answer: \(0\).

retry.feedback: Substitute the given coordinates after integrating. They determine C.

sections.intro: A given coordinate fixes the vertical shift. Substitute both coordinates after integrating, and then solve for the constant.

examples.title: Recover a curve from its gradient
examples.question: A curve has gradient \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=6x-4\). Find its general equation.
solution: Reverse the power rule on \(6x\): the exponent rises from \(1\) to \(2\), so the term becomes \(\frac{6}{2}x^2=3x^2\).
Since \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(-4x)=-4\), the constant gradient term contributes \(-4x\).
Write \(y=3x^2-4x+C\). Differentiating returns \(6x-4\) for every value of \(C\).

examples.title: Recover a curve from a negative fractional gradient
examples.question: A curve with \(x>0\) has gradient \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\frac{2}{x^2}\). Find its equation if it passes through \((2,5)\).
solution: Rewrite the gradient as \(-2x^{-2}\). Integration raises the exponent to \(-1\) and divides its coefficient by \(-1\).
The general equation is \(y=2x^{-1}+C\). The point gives \(5=2(2)^{-1}+C=1+C\), so \(C=4\).
The curve is \(y=\frac2x+4\). Its derivative is \(-\frac2{x^2}\) and at \(x=2\) its value is \(5\).

examples.title: Compare two curves with the same gradient
examples.question: The curves \(y=x^2-1\) and \(y=x^2+3\) have the same gradient function. Explain why and find their vertical separation.
solution: Differentiate each formula. The derivative of either constant is zero, so both gradient functions are \(2x\).
Subtract the two ordinates at the same \(x\): \((x^2+3)-(x^2-1)=4\).
The separation is \(4\) units at every \(x\). In the family \(y=x^2+C\), changing \(C\) moves the curve vertically.

examples.title: Check which curve belongs to a gradient family
examples.question: The gradient function is \(4x\). Decide which of \(y=2x^2-3\), \(y=4x^2+3\) and \(y=2x^2+x\) lies in the family of curves with this gradient.
solution: The derivative of the first curve is \(4x\). The derivative of its constant term is zero.
The other derivatives are \(8x\) and \(4x+1\). A change to the coefficient of \(x^2\) or the addition of an \(x\) term changes the gradient function.
Only \(y=2x^2-3\) lies in the family \(y=2x^2+C\).

examples.title: Use an off-axis point to fix the constant
examples.question: A curve satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4x-1\) and passes through \((-1,5)\). Find its equation.
solution: Integrate each term to get \(y=2x^2-x+C\). The gradient alone leaves \(C\) undetermined.
Substitute both coordinates: \(5=2(-1)^2-(-1)+C=3+C\). Hence \(C=2\).
The curve is \(y=2x^2-x+2\). At \(x=-1\) its value is \(2+1+2=5\).

examples.title: Use a known point to predict a second height
examples.question: A curve has gradient \(6x^2-2\) and passes through \((1,4)\). Find its y-coordinate at \(x=-1\).
solution: Integrating each term gives \(y=2x^3-2x+C\). At \(x=1\) the two variable terms cancel, giving \(C=4\).
The two points have the same height. They lie in different places on the same curve.

revision.body:
What is being reversed?

Integration reverses differentiation by finding functions with the specified derivative.

Why is there an arbitrary constant?

Adding any constant makes a vertical translation whose derivative is unchanged.

How does a point select one curve?

A point gives an input and output for the antiderivative.

Quick worked example

A curve has gradient \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=6x-4\). Find its general equation.

Reverse the power rule on \(6x\): the exponent rises from \(1\) to \(2\), so the term becomes \(\frac{6}{2}x^2=3x^2\).

Since \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(-4x)=-4\), the constant gradient term contributes \(-4x\).

Write \(y=3x^2-4x+C\). Differentiating returns \(6x-4\) for every value of \(C\).

addmaths-0606-int-indefinite.description: Integrate sums of powers, simplifiable quotients and rational powers with the correct restrictions.

sections.title: What happens to an exponent when integrating?
sections.label: Raise power

blocks.html:
For \(n\ne-1\), add one to the exponent n and then divide by the new exponent.

\(\int ax^n\,\mathrm dx=\frac{a}{n+1}x^{n+1}+C,\qquad n\ne-1.\)

figure.alt: The cubic and its parabolic derivative meet at zero. The derivative is also zero there.
figure.caption: For the blue curve \(F(x)=x^3\), the green graph gives \(F'(x)=3x^2\). The green graph stays on or above the x-axis, so the blue curve has non-negative gradient.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Integrate term by term. Add a single arbitrary constant at the end.

Think of a constant as \(ax^0\). Its new exponent is one, so its contribution is \(ax\). This differs from differentiation, where the derivative of a constant is zero.

blocks.title: Integrate powers and use a point to fix the constant
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(4 x^{2} - x - 1\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Add one to each exponent, divide by the new exponent and handle an exponent of −1 separately.
blocks.solution:
Integrate each power after simplifying.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(4 x^{2} - x - 1\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{4 x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{2}}{2} - x\).

retry.feedback: The integral of a constant is a linear term. The arbitrary constant is in addition to that term.

blocks.html: Dividing by the old exponent does not reverse the power rule.

blocks.title: Use the new exponent as the divisor
blocks.prompt: Write the integral of \(3x^3\) as \(kx^4+C\). Find the exact value of \(k\).
blocks.hint: Raise the exponent from three to four, and divide by four.
blocks.solution: \(\int 3x^3\,\mathrm dx=\frac34 x^4+C\). The derivative of \(\frac34 x^4\) is \(3x^3\).

sections.intro: For a power of x, add one to the exponent and divide by the new exponent. Differentiate your result to check both the exponent and the coefficient.

sections.title: How do you integrate roots and negative powers?
sections.label: Fractional powers

blocks.html:
Rewrite a root or reciprocal as a rational power. Keep the original domain.

On \(x>0\), write \(\sqrt{x}=x^{1/2}\) and \(\frac1{x^2}=x^{-2}\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Increase the exponent by one, then divide by that new value, provided it is non-zero.

Compute the new exponent before changing the coefficient. For \(x^{-2}\) this is \(-1\), giving \(-x^{-1}\). For \(x^{-1}\) itself the rule has a zero denominator, so use a logarithm.

blocks.title: Integrate powers and use a point to fix the constant
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(3 \sqrt{x} + 6 + \frac{5}{x^{2}}\). Work on \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Add one to each exponent, divide by the new exponent and handle an exponent of −1 separately.
blocks.solution:
Integrate each power after simplifying.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(3 \sqrt{x} + 6 + \frac{5}{x^{2}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 2 x^{\frac{3}{2}} + 6 x - \frac{5}{x}\).

retry.feedback: The integral of a constant is a linear term. The arbitrary constant is in addition to that term.

blocks.html: For a reciprocal squared, the new exponent is negative one rather than zero.

blocks.title: Keep the sign of a negative exponent
blocks.prompt: For \(x>0\), an integral of \(6x^{-3}\) has form \(k x^{-2}+C\). Find \(k\).
blocks.hint: The new exponent is \(-2\). Divide the coefficient by this value.
blocks.solution: \(\frac6{-2}=-3\). Checking, \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(-3x^{-2})=6x^{-3}\).

retry.feedback: The new exponent is negative. Dividing by it makes the antiderivative coefficient negative.

sections.intro: Rewrite roots and reciprocal powers before using the rule. For example, \(\sqrt{x}=x^{1/2}\) integrates to \(\frac23 x^{3/2}+C\).

sections.title: When is it helpful to divide a quotient term by term?
sections.label: Simplify first

blocks.html:
Expanding a short square and dividing each term by the denominator can reveal standard integrands.

\(\frac{p(x)+q(x)}{x^m}=\frac{p(x)}{x^m}+\frac{q(x)}{x^m}\quad (x^m\ne0).\)

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Simplify the integrand. Integrate a reciprocal x term as a natural logarithm on the appropriate domain.

Expand a short power in the numerator when it makes division easier. Reduce each power before integrating. For example, dividing \(3x^4\) by \(x^3\) leaves \(3x\).

blocks.title: Integrate powers and use a point to fix the constant
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(\frac{\left(9 x + 9\right)^{2}}{x^{2}}\). Work on \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Add one to each exponent, divide by the new exponent and handle an exponent of −1 separately.
blocks.solution:
Expand and divide each term by \(x^2\) to write the integrand as \(81 + \frac{162}{x} + \frac{81}{x^{2}}\). The \(\frac{1}{x}\) term integrates to a logarithm on the positive domain.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{\left(9 x + 9\right)^{2}}{x^{2}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 81 x + 162 \ln{\left(x \right)} - \frac{81}{x}\).

retry.feedback: The integral of a constant is a linear term. The arbitrary constant is in addition to that term.

blocks.html: Do not integrate the numerator and denominator separately.

blocks.title: Find the term that produces a logarithm
blocks.prompt: For \(x>0\), \(\int\frac{2x^3+5x-2}{x^2}\,\mathrm dx=x^2+k\ln x+\frac2x+C\). Find \(k\).
blocks.hint: Divide each numerator term by \(x^2\). Which term has power \(-1\)?
blocks.solution: The middle term is \(5x^{-1}\). This integrates to \(5\ln x\) on \(x>0\), so \(k=5\).

blocks.html: The power rule has an exception at exponent −1. Check the simplified integrand before using it.

sections.intro: First cancel common factors or distribute division so each term has a recognizable form. Watch for a reciprocal term, which uses a logarithm.

examples.title: Use the power rule term by term
examples.question: Find \(\int(8x^3-6x+5)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: On the cubic, raise the exponent and divide by the new exponent: \(8x^3\) contributes \(\frac{8}{4}x^4=2x^4\).
The linear term contributes \(-\frac{6}{2}x^2=-3x^2\). The constant term contributes \(5x\).
The complete integral is \(2x^4-3x^2+5x+C\). Differentiation returns the original three terms.

examples.title: Add one before dividing by the new power
examples.question: Find \(\int\left(12 x^{2} - 8 x - 3\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: For \(12x^2\), the new power is three, giving \(\frac{12}{3}x^3=4x^3\).
For \(-8x\), the new power is two, giving \(-4x^2\). The constant \(-3\) contributes \(-3x\).
The full family is \(4 x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - 3 x+C\). Differentiate this expression to recover \(12 x^{2} - 8 x - 3\). Every value of \(C\) gives the same derivative.

examples.title: Handle a root and a reciprocal power
examples.question: Find \(\int\left(3\sqrt{x}+\frac{4}{x^2}\right)\mathrm dx\) for \(x>0\).
solution: Rewrite the integrand as \(3x^{1/2}+4x^{-2}\). The positive domain makes the root and reciprocal well-defined.
For the root, divide by \(\frac32\) to obtain \(2x^{3/2}\). For \(x^{-2}\), divide by \(-1\) to obtain \(-4x^{-1}\).
The result is \(2x^{3/2}-\frac{4}{x}+C\). The derivative of the negative reciprocal gives a positive \(4x^{-2}\).

examples.title: Handle two different positive fractional powers

The other exponent becomes \(\frac13+1=\frac43\). Its new coefficient is \(\frac{-3}{4/3}=-\frac94\).

Integrate the terms separately. The middle term has exponent \(-1\), so it gives \(4\ln x\) on this domain.

examples.title: Cancel powers before applying different rules

solution: Divide each numerator term by \(x^3\). This gives \(3x+2x^{-1}-6x^{-3}\).
The terms \(3x\) and \(-6x^{-3}\) use the power rule. Integrate them to \(\frac32 x^2\) and \(3x^{-2}\), respectively.
For the reciprocal term, the exponent is \(-1\). Its integral is \(2\ln x\) on the positive branch.

The full family is \(\frac{3 x^{2}}{2} + 2 \log{\left(x \right)} + \frac{3}{x^{2}}+C\). Differentiate this expression to recover \(3 x + \frac{2}{x} - \frac{6}{x^{3}}\). Every value of \(C\) gives the same derivative.

revision.body:
What happens to an exponent when integrating?

For \(n\ne-1\), add one to the exponent n and then divide by the new exponent.

How do you integrate roots and negative powers?

Rewrite a root or reciprocal as a rational power. Keep the original domain.

When is it helpful to divide a quotient term by term?

Expanding a short square and dividing each term by the denominator can reveal standard integrands.

Quick worked example

Find \(\int(8x^3-6x+5)\,\mathrm dx\).

On the cubic, raise the exponent and divide by the new exponent: \(8x^3\) contributes \(\frac{8}{4}x^4=2x^4\).

The linear term contributes \(-\frac{6}{2}x^2=-3x^2\). The constant term contributes \(5x\).

The complete integral is \(2x^4-3x^2+5x+C\). Differentiation returns the original three terms.
revision.checks:
• Dividing by the old exponent does not reverse the power rule.
  • For a reciprocal squared, the new exponent is negative one rather than zero.
revision.examTip: The power rule has an exception at exponent −1. Check the simplified integrand before using it.

addmaths-0606-int-linear-power.description: Integrate positive, negative and fractional powers of a linear bracket using the reverse chain factor.

sections.title: Why divide by the inner slope?
sections.label: Linear factor

blocks.html:
Differentiating a power of a linear bracket multiplies by the derivative of the bracket.

\(\int k(ax+b)^n\,\mathrm dx=\frac{k(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C\quad(a\ne0,\ n\ne-1).\)

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Use the ordinary integration power rule on the bracket and divide by the inner slope.

The outer derivative would multiply by \(n+1\). The inner derivative would multiply by \(a\). Divide by both factors when finding the antiderivative. Include a negative sign if one of the factors is negative.

blocks.title: Integrate a power of a linear expression
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(2 \left(2 x + 9\right)^{4}\) on the interval where \(2 x + 9>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Check which constant appears when differentiating the bracket.
blocks.solution:
Raise the bracket power by one and divide by that new power and by the inner coefficient \(2\).

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(2 \left(2 x + 9\right)^{4}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{\left(2 x + 9\right)^{5}}{5}\).

retry.feedback: The integrated power needs the reciprocal of the inner derivative as well as division by the new exponent.

blocks.html: The inner slope is a constant, but it still affects the factor.

blocks.title: Divide by a negative inner gradient
blocks.hint: The derivative of \((7-2x)^4\) brings down two factors: the four and the inner gradient \(-2\).
blocks.solution: Matching the coefficient gives \(4(-2)k=12\), so \(k=-\frac32\).

sections.intro: Keep the inner expression in brackets. The reverse chain rule divides by its constant derivative, as well as the new power.

sections.title: How do you handle a fractional bracket power?
sections.label: Roots

blocks.html:
The new power can still be fractional. Work on the interval where the expression is real.

\(\int k\sqrt{ax+b}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{2k}{3a}(ax+b)^{3/2}+C\) where the root is real and \(a\ne0\).

figure.caption: This is \(y=3\sqrt{2x+1}\) from the first worked example. The enclosed region has x-limits \(0\) and \(4\). The expression \(2x+1\) takes the values \(1\) and \(9\).

blocks.html:

For definite integrals, calculate the two values of the bracket before taking the powers. A value such as \(9^{3/2}\) is easy to read as \((\sqrt9)^3=27\).

examples.title: Keep the linear bracket
examples.question: Find \(\int 6(2x+1)^2\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: Raise the bracket exponent from \(2\) to \(3\). Differentiating \((2x+1)^3\) would give \(3(2x+1)^2\) times the inner derivative \(2\).
The coefficient needed in front is \(\frac{6}{3\times2}=1\). The result is \((2x+1)^3+C\).
Check: its derivative is \(3(2x+1)^2\cdot2=6(2x+1)^2\).

examples.title: Keep a descending linear bracket
examples.question: Find \(\int\left(6 \left(5 - 2 x\right)^{2}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: Keep \(5-2x\) together and increase the outer power to three.
Divide by the new outer exponent \(3\) and the inner derivative \(-2\). The coefficient is \(\frac6{3(-2)}=-1\).
The full family is \(- \left(5 - 2 x\right)^{3}+C\). Differentiate this expression to recover \(6 \left(5 - 2 x\right)^{2}\). Every value of \(C\) gives the same derivative.

examples.title: Choose bounds that simplify a square root
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^4 3\sqrt{2x+1}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The bracket has derivative \(2\). Increasing the exponent to \(\frac32\) gives coefficient \(\frac{3}{2\times\frac32}=1\).
Use \(F(x)=(2x+1)^{3/2}\). At \(x=0\) the bracket is \(1\), and at \(x=4\) it is \(9\).

examples.title: Use both limits with a square-root bracket
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{1}\left(6 \sqrt{3 x + 1}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Rewrite the root as a half power. The new exponent is \(\frac32\), and the bracket's gradient is \(3\). The coefficient becomes \(\frac6{(3/2)\cdot3}=\frac43\).
At the two x-values the bracket equals \(1\) and \(4\), so its powers are \(1^{3/2}=1\) and \(4^{3/2}=8\).
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=\frac{4 \left(3 x + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(1)=\frac{32}{3}\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=\frac{4}{3}\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(1)-F(0)=\frac{32}{3}-\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)=\frac{28}{3}\).

examples.title: Read the sign of a negative bracket power
examples.question: Find \(\int \frac{12}{(3x+1)^3}\,\mathrm dx\) on \(x>-\frac13\).
solution: The power is \(-3\). Raise it to \(-2\) and divide the coefficient by both \(-2\) and the inner derivative \(3\).
The result is \(-2(3x+1)^{-2}+C\). The coefficient is negative because the new power is negative.

examples.title: Evaluate a reciprocal-square integral with small bounds
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\frac{8}{\left(2 x + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The bracket is positive over this interval. Write the power as \(-2\) and add one to get \(-1\).
Divide \(8\) by \(-1\) and by the inner gradient \(2\). The coefficient is \(-4\).
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=- \frac{4}{2 x + 1}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(\frac{1}{2})=-2\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=-4\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(\frac{1}{2})-F(0)=-2-\left(-4\right)=2\).

revision.body:
Why divide by the inner slope?

Differentiating a power of a linear bracket multiplies by the derivative of the bracket.

How do you handle a fractional bracket power?

The new power can still be fractional. Work on the interval where the expression is real.

How does a negative bracket power integrate?

Add one to the exponent and check the result is non-zero.

Quick worked example

Find \(\int 6(2x+1)^2\,\mathrm dx\).

Raise the bracket exponent from \(2\) to \(3\). Differentiating \((2x+1)^3\) would give \(3(2x+1)^2\) times the inner derivative \(2\).

The coefficient needed in front is \(\frac{6}{3\times2}=1\). The result is \((2x+1)^3+C\).

Check: its derivative is \(3(2x+1)^2\cdot2=6(2x+1)^2\).

sections.title: What stays when an exponential integrates?
sections.label: Keep exponential

blocks.html:
An exponential with a linear exponent stays exponential.

\(\int k e^{ax+b}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{k}{a}e^{ax+b}+C\quad(a\ne0).\)

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Keep the exponent unchanged and divide by its x-coefficient.

The exponent \(ax+b\) is unchanged. Differentiating multiplies by \(a\), so integration divides the outside coefficient by \(a\). The shift \(b\) remains inside the exponent.

blocks.title: Integrate an exponential expression and evaluate its net change
blocks.prompt:
Take the integrand \(7 e^{6 x + 2}\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Differentiate your proposed antiderivative to check the multiplier.
blocks.solution:
Keep the exponential and divide by the coefficient \(6\) of x in its exponent.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(7 e^{6 x + 2}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{7 e^{6 x + 2}}{6}\).

retry.feedback: Integration divides by the derivative of the linear exponent rather than multiplying by it.

blocks.html: Changing the exponent itself gives a different derivative.

blocks.title: Find the multiplier of a shifted exponential
blocks.prompt: \(\int 15e^{3x+1}\,\mathrm dx=k e^{3x+1}+C\). Find \(k\).
blocks.hint: The shift \(+1\) stays in the exponent. Its derivative is zero, so the inner gradient is \(3\).
blocks.solution: Differentiating \(k e^{3x+1}\) gives \(3k e^{3x+1}\). Hence \(3k=15\), so \(k=5\).

sections.intro: Look inside the exponential. Its exponent stays the same in the integral, while division by the exponent's derivative cancels the chain-rule factor.

sections.title: What if the exponent's slope is negative?
sections.label: Negative exponent

blocks.html:
Dividing by the negative inner slope creates a negative coefficient.

\(\int_0^t R(s)\,\mathrm ds\) accumulates the quantity delivered by a rate \(R\).

figure.alt: A decreasing positive flow rate with the area between times zero and one shaded.
figure.caption: The height is the rate \(R(t)=6e^{-2t}\) in litres per minute. The shaded region from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\) measures the volume delivered, in litres.

sections.title: How do you integrate an exponential with other terms?
sections.label: Exponential sums

blocks.html:
Use the appropriate antiderivative term by term.

\(\int(c+ke^{ax+b})\,\mathrm dx=cx+\frac{k}{a}e^{ax+b}+C.\)

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Keep exact exponentials until a decimal answer is requested. Include the arbitrary constant for an indefinite integral.

Before rounding, substitute both limits into the complete expression. At a zero exponent \(e^0=1\). This still contributes to the value of the antiderivative.

blocks.title: Combine a constant and an exponential exactly
blocks.prompt: The exact value of \(\int_0^{\frac12}\bigl(4+6e^{2x}\bigr)\,\mathrm dx\) is \(a+be\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are integers. Find both coefficients.
blocks.hint: Find the antiderivative of both terms. Keep the constant contribution and the coefficient of \(e\) separate.
blocks.solution:
The antiderivative is \(4x+3e^{2x}\). At \(\frac12\) it gives \(2+3e\), and at zero it gives \(3\).

The difference is \((2+3e)-3=-1+3e\). Thus \(a=-1\) and \(b=3\).

examples.title: Find the multiplier of an exponential
examples.question: Find \(\int 12e^{3x-1}\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: Differentiating \(e^{3x-1}\) keeps the same exponential and multiplies it by \(3\).
Use coefficient \(\frac{12}{3}=4\), giving \(4e^{3x-1}+C\).
Differentiate to check: \(4\cdot3e^{3x-1}=12e^{3x-1}\).

examples.title: Evaluate an exponential at inputs with simple exponents
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{1}^{2}\left(4 e^{2 x - 2}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The exponent stays \(2x-2\). Divide the coefficient by the derivative of that exponent, giving \(\frac42=2\).
The exponent is zero at the lower limit and two at the upper limit.
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=2 e^{2 x - 2}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(2)=2 e^{2}\). The written lower limit gives \(F(1)=2\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(2)-F(1)=2 e^{2}-\left(2\right)=-2 + 2 e^{2}\).

examples.title: Integrate exponential decay over a time interval
examples.question: A flow rate is \(R(t)=6e^{-2t}\) litres per minute. Find the volume delivered between \(t=0\) and \(t=1\) minute.
solution: The antiderivative of the rate is \(-3e^{-2t}\). The factor \(-3\) comes from dividing by the inner derivative \(-2\).
Subtract the lower endpoint value: \(-3e^{-2}-(-3)=3(1-e^{-2})\).
The volume is \(3(1-e^{-2})\) litres, about \(2.59\) litres. It is positive because the rate stays positive.

examples.title: Track the sign for a decaying exponential
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\frac{2}{3}}\left(3 e^{- 3 x}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Differentiate the exponent \(-3x\) to get \(-3\). Divide the integrand coefficient \(3\) by \(-3\), giving a negative antiderivative.
The integrand is positive throughout the interval. Expect a positive definite integral after subtracting.
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=- e^{- 3 x}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(\frac{2}{3})=- \frac{1}{e^{2}}\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=-1\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(\frac{2}{3})-F(0)=- \frac{1}{e^{2}}-\left(-1\right)=1 - e^{-2}\).

examples.title: Combine exponentials with different inner slopes
examples.question: Find \(\int(6e^{2x}+4e^{-x})\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: Integrate the first term using inner derivative \(2\). Its contribution is \(3e^{2x}\).
Integrate the second using inner derivative \(-1\). Its contribution is \(-4e^{-x}\).
The result is \(3e^{2x}-4e^{-x}+C\). Differentiating the second term gives \(+4e^{-x}\).

examples.title: Combine a fixed rate with a decreasing term
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{1}\left(1 + 4 e^{- 2 x}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Integrate the constant \(1\) to \(x\). For \(4e^{-2x}\), keep the exponent and divide by \(-2\).
Evaluate the sum at each endpoint. At the lower limit the exponential contributes \(-2\) because \(e^0=1\).
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=x - 2 e^{- 2 x}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(1)=1 - \frac{2}{e^{2}}\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=-2\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(1)-F(0)=1 - \frac{2}{e^{2}}-\left(-2\right)=3 - \frac{2}{e^{2}}\).

blocks.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(11 \sin{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{5} \right)} - 2\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Differentiate negative cosine to check the sign. The inner angle has gradient 2, so the antiderivative needs a factor of one half.
blocks.solution:
The antiderivative of sine is negative cosine. Then divide by the inner derivative.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(11 \sin{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{5} \right)} - 2\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C - 2 x - \frac{11 \cos{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{5} \right)}}{2}\).

retry.feedback: Differentiate the proposed expression. Check the inner angle's multiplier and the derivative of any separate linear term.

blocks.html: Cosine without the negative sign differentiates to negative sine.

blocks.title: Include the minus sign and the inner factor
blocks.prompt: \(\int9\sin(6x)\,\mathrm dx=k\cos(6x)+C\). Angles are in radians. Find \(k\).
blocks.hint: The derivative of \(\cos(6x)\) is \(-6\sin(6x)\).
blocks.solution: Matching coefficients gives \(-6k=9\), so \(k=-\frac32\).

sections.intro: Choose an antiderivative by differentiating back. Negative cosine gives positive sine, and a linear angle introduces an extra derivative factor.

sections.title: Which antiderivative gives cosine?
sections.label: Cosine to sine

blocks.html:
Sine differentiates to cosine in radian measure.

\(\int k\cos(ax+b)\,\mathrm dx=\frac{k}{a}\sin(ax+b)+C\quad(a\ne0).\)

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Use the same angle inside sine and divide by the inner derivative. Combine with the integral of any constant term.

Substitute limits into the angle before evaluating the sine. For \(3x+\frac\pi6\) at \(x=\frac\pi9\), the angle is \(\frac\pi3+\frac\pi6=\frac\pi2\).

blocks.title: Your turn
blocks.prompt: Write \(\int 12\cos(4x)\,\mathrm dx=A\sin(4x)+C\). Find \(A\) in radian measure.
blocks.hint: Differentiate the proposed answer. What multiplies the cosine when the angle is \(4x\)?
blocks.solution: Differentiating gives \(4A\cos(4x)\). Matching coefficients gives \(4A=12\), so \(A=3\).

retry.feedback: The derivative of \(\sin(4x)\) includes the inner factor \(4\). Divide \(12\) by \(4\).

blocks.title: Match a cosine to its antiderivative
blocks.prompt: Which is the complete family of antiderivatives of \(6\cos(3x)-2\)? Angles are in radians.
blocks.hint: Cosine integrates to sine. Include the factor from its inner angle.
blocks.solution: Differentiating \(2\sin(3x)-2x+C\) gives \(6\cos(3x)-2\). The arbitrary constant \(C\) allows the whole family.

blocks.html: A constant term integrates to a multiple of x.

blocks.title: Use sine values at a shifted angle
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{- \frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{12}}\left(4 \cos{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
blocks.hint: The angle is zero at the first limit and \(\frac\pi2\) at the second.
blocks.solution:
Divide the coefficient by the inner gradient \(2\), then evaluate the sine at both angles.

Use \(F(x)=2 \sin{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(0\) and \(2\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(2\).

sections.intro: Sine gives cosine when differentiated in radians. Keep the angle exactly as written and divide by its derivative when it is linear.

sections.title: How does tangent appear when integrating?
sections.label: Secant squared

blocks.html:
Tangent differentiates to secant squared when the angle is measured in radians.

\(\int k\sec^2(ax+b)\,\mathrm dx=\frac{k}{a}\tan(ax+b)+C\quad(a\ne0).\)

figure.alt: The portion of the secant-squared graph from zero to pi over six is shaded. Vertical dashed lines show the nearest poles.
figure.caption: The blue curve is \(y=4\sec^2(2x)\). The shaded interval ends at \(\frac\pi6\), before the pole at \(\frac\pi4\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Use a tangent antiderivative and choose bounds on one continuous branch.

Find the points where \(\cos(ax+b)=0\). These are excluded from the integrand. Check that the interval lies entirely between consecutive excluded points before using the tangent at the endpoints.

blocks.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(4 \sec^{2}{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Use standard sine, cosine or secant-squared antiderivatives and divide by the inner slope.
blocks.solution:
The derivative of tangent is secant squared. Divide by the factor from the bracket.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(4 \sec^{2}{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{\tan{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}}{2}\).

retry.feedback: Differentiate the proposed expression. Check the inner angle's multiplier and the derivative of any separate linear term.

blocks.html: An interval crossing a point where cosine is zero cannot be evaluated with the ordinary finite-bound formula.

blocks.title: Check the interval before using tangent
blocks.prompt: In radians, which interval stays inside one continuous branch of \(\sec^2(2x)\)?
blocks.hint: The two poles nearest zero occur where \(2x=\pm\frac\pi2\).
blocks.solution: The poles are at \(x=\pm\frac\pi4\). The interval \(\left[0,\frac\pi6\right]\) stays strictly between them.

blocks.html: Use radians throughout and retain exact special-angle values where the question asks for an exact result.

sections.intro: Tangent gives secant squared. For definite integration check that tangent is continuous between the two endpoints before subtracting.

examples.title: Integrate sine using negative cosine
examples.question: Find \(\int(8\sin(4x)-3)\,\mathrm dx\). Use radians.
solution: Differentiate \(-\cos(4x)\) to get \(4\sin(4x)\). The minus sign gives a positive sine.
The coefficient needed is \(\frac84=2\). The constant term gives \(-3x\).
The result is \(-2\cos(4x)-3x+C\). Differentiating gives \(8\sin(4x)-3\).

examples.title: Use the cosine sign at the end of a sine interval
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly. Angles are in radians.
solution: The derivative of \(-\cos(2x)\) is \(2\sin(2x)\). The minus sign and the inner factor are both present.
The angle changes from \(0\) to \(\frac\pi2\), where cosine equals \(1\) and \(0\).
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=- \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(\frac{\pi}{4})=0\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=-1\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(\frac{\pi}{4})-F(0)=0-\left(-1\right)=1\).

examples.title: Integrate a cosine with a linear angle
examples.question: Find \(\int 6\cos(3x)\,\mathrm dx\). Use radians.
solution: Sine differentiates to cosine. Keeping the angle \(3x\) in the sine multiplies its derivative by \(3\).
Divide the coefficient \(6\) by \(3\), giving \(2\sin(3x)+C\).
Check: \(2\cdot3\cos(3x)=6\cos(3x)\). For a sine integrand the corresponding primitive uses negative cosine.

examples.title: Use an offset angle at both limits
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{9}}\left(6 \cos{\left(3 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly. Angles are in radians.
solution: Cosine integrates to sine. Divide the coefficient \(6\) by the angle derivative \(3\), and keep the offset \(\frac\pi6\).
At the two endpoints the angles are \(\frac\pi6\) and \(\frac\pi2\). Their sine values are \(\frac12\) and \(1\).
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=2 \sin{\left(3 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(\frac{\pi}{9})=2\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=1\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(\frac{\pi}{9})-F(0)=2-\left(1\right)=1\).

examples.title: Evaluate a secant-squared integral on one branch
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\pi/6} 4\sec^2(2x)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The angle \(2x\) runs from \(0\) to \(\frac{\pi}{3}\), where cosine stays positive. The integral stays on one continuous branch.
An antiderivative is \(2\tan(2x)\), since differentiating \(\tan(2x)\) introduces a factor of \(2\).
Evaluate \(2\tan(\frac{\pi}{3})-2\tan(0)=2\sqrt3\).

examples.title: Evaluate tangent on a continuous branch
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{- \frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{12}}\left(3 \sec^{2}{\left(3 x \right)}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly. Angles are in radians.
solution: The derivative of \(\tan(3x)\) is \(3\sec^2(3x)\). Hence its coefficient in the antiderivative is one.
The angle ranges from \(-\frac\pi4\) to \(\frac\pi4\), wholly inside one continuous tangent branch.
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=\tan{\left(3 x \right)}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(\frac{\pi}{12})=1\). The written lower limit gives \(F(- \frac{\pi}{12})=-1\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(\frac{\pi}{12})-F(- \frac{\pi}{12})=1-\left(-1\right)=2\).

extraPractice.title: Check the sign by differentiating
extraPractice.prompt: Which is the complete family of antiderivatives of \(4\sin(2x)+1\)? Angles are in radians.
extraPractice.hint: The derivative of cosine has a negative sign. Then account for the factor of two inside the angle.
extraPractice.solution: The derivative of \(-2\cos(2x)+x+C\) is \(4\sin(2x)+1\).

extraPractice.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
extraPractice.prompt:
The integrand is \(- 7 \cos{\left(7 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} - 3\). Angles are in radians.

Evaluate \(\int_{\frac{\pi}{49}}^{\frac{25 \pi}{196}}- 7 \cos{\left(7 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} - 3\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Use standard sine, cosine or secant-squared antiderivatives and divide by the inner slope.
extraPractice.solution:
The variable part of an antiderivative is \(- 3 x - \sin{\left(7 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}\).

Subtract its value at \(\frac{\pi}{49}\) from its value at \(\frac{25 \pi}{196}\).

Answer: \(- \frac{9 \pi}{28} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + 1\).

retry.feedback: A derivative check catches the sign of the cosine antiderivative and the chain factor.

extraPractice.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
extraPractice.prompt:
The integrand is \(8 \cos{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} + 4\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
extraPractice.hint: Use standard sine, cosine or secant-squared antiderivatives and divide by the inner slope.
extraPractice.solution:
Cosine integrates to sine. Divide the sine coefficient by the inner derivative.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(8 \cos{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} + 4\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 4 x + 4 \sin{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}\).

extraPractice.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
extraPractice.prompt:
The integrand is \(8 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} - 3\). Angles are in radians.

Evaluate \(\int_{\frac{\pi}{56}}^{\frac{5 \pi}{84}}8 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} - 3\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Use standard sine, cosine or secant-squared antiderivatives and divide by the inner slope.
extraPractice.solution:
The variable part of an antiderivative is \(- 3 x - \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}\).

Subtract its value at \(\frac{\pi}{56}\) from its value at \(\frac{5 \pi}{84}\).

Answer: \(- \frac{\pi}{8} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

retry.feedback: A derivative check catches the sign of the cosine antiderivative and the chain factor.

extraPractice.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
extraPractice.prompt:
The integrand is \(11 \sec^{2}{\left(4 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)} - 3\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
extraPractice.hint: Use standard sine, cosine or secant-squared antiderivatives and divide by the inner slope.
extraPractice.solution:

extraPractice.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
extraPractice.prompt:
The integrand is \(6 \sec^{2}{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} + 3\). Angles are in radians.

Evaluate \(\int_{- \frac{\pi}{12}}^{0}6 \sec^{2}{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} + 3\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Use standard sine, cosine or secant-squared antiderivatives and divide by the inner slope.

The variable part of an antiderivative is \(3 x + 3 \tan{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}\).

Subtract its value at \(- \frac{\pi}{12}\) from its value at \(0\).

Answer: \(\frac{\pi}{4} + \sqrt{3}\).

revision.body:
Which antiderivative gives sine?

The derivative of \(-\cos x\) is \(\sin x\).

Which antiderivative gives cosine?

Sine differentiates to cosine in radian measure.

How does tangent appear when integrating?

Tangent differentiates to secant squared when the angle is measured in radians.

Quick worked example

Find \(\int 6\cos(3x)\,\mathrm dx\). Use radians.

Sine differentiates to cosine. Keeping the angle \(3x\) in the sine multiplies its derivative by \(3\).

Divide the coefficient \(6\) by \(3\), giving \(2\sin(3x)+C\).

Check: \(2\cdot3\cos(3x)=6\cos(3x)\). For a sine integrand the corresponding primitive uses negative cosine.
revision.checks:
• Cosine without the negative sign differentiates to negative sine.
  • A constant term integrates to a multiple of x.

addmaths-0606-int-logarithmic.description: Recognise the power-rule exception and choose a logarithmic form on a valid interval.

sections.title: Why does one over x need a different rule?
sections.label: Exception

blocks.html:
For \(x>0\), differentiating \(\ln x\) gives \(\frac1x\).

\(\int \frac{k}{x}\,\mathrm dx=k\ln|x|+C\) on either branch of \(x\ne0\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Use a natural logarithm instead of the integration power rule at exponent −1.

A natural logarithm needs a positive argument. The absolute value makes it work on the negative branch as well. Choose the expression suitable for the domain given.

blocks.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(\frac{11}{x}\). Work on \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Confirm the denominator never reaches zero between the limits.
blocks.solution:
The integral power rule excludes exponent −1. Use a logarithm and keep the reciprocal of the linear gradient.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{11}{x}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(11\ln\left|x\right|+C\).

retry.feedback: The ordinary integration power rule fails when the new exponent would be zero. A logarithm handles that case.

blocks.html: Adding one to −1 would give a zero denominator in the power rule.

blocks.title: Combine two logarithms in exact form
blocks.prompt: \(\int_2^{10}\frac4x\,\mathrm dx=4\ln r\). Find \(r\).
blocks.hint: Subtract \(4\ln 2\) from \(4\ln 10\). The log law turns subtraction into division.
blocks.solution: The answer is \(4\ln\left(\frac{10}{2}\right)=4\ln5\), so \(r=5\).

sections.intro: An exponent of minus one would give zero in the denominator of the power rule. The derivative of a natural logarithm gives the required reciprocal instead.

sections.title: What factor goes before the logarithm?
sections.label: Linear denominator

blocks.html:
The derivative of the denominator is part of the chain rule for a logarithm.

\(\int\frac{k}{ax+b}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{k}{a}\ln|ax+b|+C\quad(a\ne0).\)

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
For a linear denominator, divide by its x-coefficient and place its absolute value inside the logarithm.

Compare the numerator with the derivative of the denominator. For \(5-2x\) that derivative is \(-2\), so a numerator of \(4\) needs a multiplier \(\frac4{-2}=-2\).

blocks.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(\frac{2}{6 x + 2}\). Work on \(6 x + 2>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Confirm the denominator never reaches zero between the limits.
blocks.solution:
The integral power rule excludes exponent −1. Use a logarithm and keep the reciprocal of the linear gradient.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{2}{6 x + 2}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(\frac{1}{3}\ln\left|6 x + 2\right|+C\).

retry.feedback: The ordinary integration power rule fails when the new exponent would be zero. A logarithm handles that case.

blocks.html: A logarithmic antiderivative of a reciprocal has a factor from the denominator.

blocks.title: Divide by a negative denominator gradient
blocks.prompt: For \(x<4\), write \(\int\frac{3}{8-2x}\,\mathrm dx=k\ln(8-2x)+C\). Find \(k\).
blocks.hint: Differentiating \(\ln(8-2x)\) produces \(-2\) in the numerator.
blocks.solution: The numerator condition is \(-2k=3\), hence \(k=-\frac32\).

sections.intro: Write the reciprocal as a constant times one over a linear expression. The inner derivative supplies the additional factor you must divide by.

sections.title: Why must both limits stay on the same side of a pole?
sections.label: Single branch

blocks.html:
A reciprocal is not continuous where its denominator is zero.

On one continuous branch, \(\ln|u(b)|-\ln|u(a)|=\ln\left(\frac{|u(b)|}{|u(a)|}\right)\).

figure.alt: A reciprocal graph with dashed vertical asymptote x equals negative one. The shaded interval is to the left of the asymptote.
figure.caption: For \(y=\frac1{x+1}\), the shaded interval \([-3,-2]\) stays on the negative branch. The dashed line is the pole at \(x=-1\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Check that the full interval lies in one continuous branch. Use the log form on that branch.

Check the denominator on the whole interval. If it vanishes between the limits, finite endpoint values on different branches do not justify a single subtraction.

blocks.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(3 + \frac{5}{7 x + 8}\). Work on \(7 x + 8<0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Confirm the denominator never reaches zero between the limits.
blocks.solution:
The integral power rule excludes exponent −1. Use a logarithm and keep the reciprocal of the linear gradient.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(3 + \frac{5}{7 x + 8}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(\frac{5}{7}\ln\left|7 x + 8\right|+3 x+C\).

retry.feedback: The ordinary integration power rule fails when the new exponent would be zero. A logarithm handles that case.

blocks.html: Two finite endpoint logarithms alone cannot justify an integral across a pole.

blocks.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(4 + \frac{4}{6 x + 7}\). Work on \(6 x + 7<0\).

Evaluate \(\int_{- \frac{23}{6}}^{- \frac{3}{2}}4 + \frac{4}{6 x + 7}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.

sections.intro: An antiderivative involving a logarithm can be used on either side of a pole, separately. The endpoint rule requires a continuous integrand between the limits.

examples.title: Use a natural logarithm for the reciprocal
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_1^4 \frac{2}{x}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The power rule would divide by zero at exponent \(-1\). On \(x>0\), the derivative of \(\ln x\) is \(\frac1x\).
Use \(F(x)=2\ln x\) and subtract \(F(4)-F(1)=2\ln4-2\ln1\).
Since \(\ln1=0\), the exact value is \(2\ln4\). Keeping the coefficient outside gives a compact exact answer.

examples.title: Simplify a log difference using a ratio
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{2}^{6}\left(\frac{3}{x}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The power rule would give a zero denominator. On \(x>0\), use \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\ln x=\frac1x\).
After substituting, the difference of logarithms can be written as \(3\ln\left(\frac62\right)=3\ln 3\).
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=3 \log{\left(x \right)}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(6)=\log{\left(216 \right)}\). The written lower limit gives \(F(2)=\log{\left(8 \right)}\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(6)-F(2)=\log{\left(216 \right)}-\left(\log{\left(8 \right)}\right)=\log{\left(27 \right)}\).

examples.title: Divide by the gradient of the denominator
examples.question: Find \(\int\frac{6}{3x+2}\,\mathrm dx\) on \(x>-\frac23\).
solution: The bracket \(3x+2\) is positive on the stated interval. Differentiate \(\ln(3x+2)\) to get \(\frac{3}{3x+2}\).
Multiply by \(\frac{6}{3}=2\), so the result is \(2\ln(3x+2)+C\).

examples.title: Match the derivative of a descending denominator
examples.question: Find \(\int\left(\frac{4}{5 - 2 x}\right)\,\mathrm dx\). Use \(x<\frac52\).
solution: The denominator stays positive on the given branch. The derivative of \(\ln(5-2x)\) is \(\frac{-2}{5-2x}\).
Multiplying that logarithm by \(\frac4{-2}=-2\) gives the required numerator.
The full family is \(- 2 \log{\left(5 - 2 x \right)}+C\). Differentiate this expression to recover \(\frac{4}{5 - 2 x}\). Every value of \(C\) gives the same derivative.

examples.title: Keep the logarithm real on a negative branch
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{-3}^{-2}\frac{1}{x+1}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Both bounds lie to the left of the pole \(x=-1\). Use \(F(x)=\ln|x+1|\) so that the input to the logarithm stays positive.
At \(x=-3\) the log input is \(2\). At \(x=-2\) it is \(1\).
The signed integral is \(\ln1-\ln2=-\ln2\). The sign agrees with the negative integrand.

examples.title: Spot a pole between two finite endpoint values
examples.question: Can the usual endpoint rule be used on \(\int_{-2}^{0}\frac{1}{x+1}\,\mathrm dx\)?
solution: The denominator vanishes at \(x=-1\), which lies between \(-2\) and \(0\). The integrand is undefined there.
The antiderivative \(\ln|x+1|\) is valid on each branch separately. Each branch ends at the pole.
The usual endpoint rule requires a continuous integrand from the lower input to the upper input. It does not apply across this pole.

revision.body:
Why does one over x need a different rule?

For \(x>0\), differentiating \(\ln x\) gives \(\frac1x\).

What factor goes before the logarithm?

The derivative of the denominator is part of the chain rule for a logarithm.

Why must both limits stay on the same side of a pole?

A reciprocal is not continuous where its denominator is zero.

Quick worked example

Evaluate \(\int_1^4 \frac{2}{x}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.

The power rule would divide by zero at exponent \(-1\). On \(x>0\), the derivative of \(\ln x\) is \(\frac1x\).

Use \(F(x)=2\ln x\) and subtract \(F(4)-F(1)=2\ln4-2\ln1\).

Since \(\ln1=0\), the exact value is \(2\ln4\). Keeping the coefficient outside gives a compact exact answer.
revision.checks:
• Adding one to −1 would give a zero denominator in the power rule.
  • A logarithmic antiderivative of a reciprocal has a factor from the denominator.

sections.title: How do you organise a sum of different function types?
sections.label: Separate terms

blocks.html:
The integral of a sum is the sum of its integrals.

If \(F'=f\) and \(G'=g\), then \(\int(f(x)+g(x))\,\mathrm dx=F(x)+G(x)+C\).

figure.alt: The blue polynomial and amber exponential add vertically to make the green sum curve.
figure.caption: The blue graph is \(6x^2\), the amber graph is \(4e^{-2x}\), and the green graph is their sum. At each input, the green height is the sum of the two component heights. Integrate each component using its own rule.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Identify an exponential, power or trigonometric rule for each term before simplifying.

Mark a different rule against each term. Integrate a power by changing its exponent, but keep the exponent of an exponential unchanged. Then add the terms and check the derivative.

blocks.title: Select the correct antiderivative for each term
blocks.prompt:
Integrate the expression \(x^{2} + 4 e^{7 x + 3}\). Any angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Choose the derivative in reverse for each term. Check your full expression by differentiation.
blocks.solution:
Integrate the terms separately, keeping each numerical coefficient with its term.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(x^{2} + 4 e^{7 x + 3}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{4 e^{7 x + 3}}{7}\).

retry.feedback: Keep one final arbitrary constant after summing the antiderivatives.

blocks.html: One power rule does not serve a sum containing different function types.

blocks.hint: The polynomial term is already integrated. Match the derivative of the cosine term to \(10\sin(5x)\).
blocks.solution: \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(k\cos(5x))=-5k\sin(5x)\). Hence \(-5k=10\) and \(k=-2\).

sections.title: How many arbitrary constants are needed?

blocks.html:

\(F(x)+C_1+G(x)+C_2=F(x)+G(x)+C\), where \(C=C_1+C_2\).

Use the given point on the combined equation. A point fixes the one total constant. Differentiation checks the method, and substitution of the point checks the constant.

blocks.title: Use a simple bracket at each limit

blocks.hint: Integrate the bracket and the constant separately. The bracket equals one at \(x=0\).
blocks.solution:
The bracket becomes a square and its coefficient divides by \(2\cdot2\). The constant contributes \(3x\).

Use \(F(x)=3 x + \left(2 x + 1\right)^{2}\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(1\) and \(12\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(11\).

blocks.html: Check all terms by differentiation, including any term that should disappear into the constant.

sections.intro: For an exponential, trigonometric or power term with a linear argument, check that you cancelled its inner derivative.

examples.title: Choose a rule separately for each term
examples.question: Find \(\int(3x^2-4e^{-2x})\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: The power term \(3x^2\) contributes \(x^3\) because its new exponent is \(3\).
The exponential term keeps exponent \(-2x\). Dividing its coefficient \(-4\) by \(-2\) gives \(2\).
The complete result is \(x^3+2e^{-2x}+C\). Its exponential derivative is negative as required.

examples.title: Use the power rule and the exponential rule together
examples.question: Find \(\int\left(6 x^{2} + 4 e^{- 2 x}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: The polynomial term \(6x^2\) integrates to \(\frac63 x^3=2x^3\).
The exponential term keeps its exponent. Divide \(4\) by the inner derivative \(-2\), giving \(-2e^{-2x}\).
The full family is \(2 x^{3} - 2 e^{- 2 x}+C\). Differentiate this expression to recover \(6 x^{2} + 4 e^{- 2 x}\). Every value of \(C\) gives the same derivative.

examples.title: Use one constant for the whole expression
examples.question: A curve has gradient \(2x+3\cos(3x)\) and passes through \((0,4)\). Find its equation.
solution: The two variable terms integrate to \(x^2\) and \(\sin(3x)\). Their arbitrary constants combine into one \(C\).
At \(x=0\) both variable terms vanish, so \(y(0)=C=4\).
Thus \(y=x^2+\sin(3x)+4\). Its derivative is \(2x+3\cos(3x)\).

examples.title: Use a single constant after combining two rules
examples.question: A curve satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=6x+4\cos(2x)\) and passes through \((0,3)\). Find its equation.
solution: Integrate the two terms separately. The results are \(3x^2\) and \(\frac42\sin(2x)=2\sin(2x)\).
Combine the terms and write one arbitrary constant: \(y=3x^2+2\sin(2x)+C\).
At \(x=0\) both variable terms are zero, so \(C=3\), giving \(y=3x^2+2\sin(2x)+3\).

examples.title: Track two different chain factors
examples.question: Find \(\int\bigl(4(2x+1)^3+3\cos(3x)\bigr)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: For the bracket power, the new exponent is \(4\) and the inner derivative is \(2\). The coefficient is \(\frac{4}{4\cdot2}=\frac12\).
For the cosine, use sine with the same angle. Its coefficient is \(\frac{3}{3}=1\).
The result is \(\frac12(2x+1)^4+\sin(3x)+C\). Differentiate the two terms separately to check.

examples.title: Combine a linear bracket with a constant term
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(12 \left(2 x + 1\right)^{2} - 5\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: For the bracket, raise the outer exponent and divide by \(3\cdot2=6\). Its contribution is \(2(2x+1)^3\).
The constant term contributes \(-5x\), so the lower evaluation still contains the bracket's value at zero.
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=- 5 x + 2 \left(2 x + 1\right)^{3}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{27}{2}\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=2\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(\frac{1}{2})-F(0)=\frac{27}{2}-\left(2\right)=\frac{23}{2}\).

revision.body:
How do you organise a sum of different function types?

The integral of a sum is the sum of its integrals.

How many arbitrary constants are needed?

All separate additive constants combine into a single constant.

When do bracketed terms need an extra factor?

A linear argument contributes its derivative on differentiation. Reverse this factor when integrating.

Quick worked example

Find \(\int(3x^2-4e^{-2x})\,\mathrm dx\).

The power term \(3x^2\) contributes \(x^3\) because its new exponent is \(3\).

The exponential term keeps exponent \(-2x\). Dividing its coefficient \(-4\) by \(-2\) gives \(2\).

The complete result is \(x^3+2e^{-2x}+C\). Its exponential derivative is negative as required.
revision.checks:
• One power rule does not serve a sum containing different function types.
  • A missing constant is incomplete for an indefinite integral.

addmaths-0606-int-definite.description: Calculate the upper antiderivative value minus the lower one and interpret a reversed interval.

sections.title: Which endpoint is subtracted?
sections.label: Upper minus lower

blocks.html:
The definite integral over a continuous interval is the antiderivative at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit.

\(\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm dx=[F(x)]_a^b=F(b)-F(a)\), where \(F'(x)=f(x)\).

figure.alt: The line crosses the x-axis at 1.5. Its larger negative region and smaller positive region are shaded between x equals negative one and two.
figure.caption: In the worked example \(y=2x-3\), both coloured regions contribute to the same definite integral. The region below the x-axis contributes a negative value.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Write both substitutions explicitly before subtracting. An antiderivative's arbitrary constant cancels.

Write \(F(b)\) and \(F(a)\) on separate lines. If the second is negative, \(-F(a)\) makes a positive contribution. A signed result below zero is possible.

blocks.title: Keep the entire lower endpoint in brackets
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{1}^{2}\left(4 x - 3\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
blocks.hint: Evaluate the same primitive at both limits. The lower evaluation is negative.
blocks.solution:
The power term gives \(2x^2\) and the constant term gives \(-3x\).

Use \(F(x)=2 x^{2} - 3 x\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(-1\) and \(2\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(3\).

blocks.html: Do not ignore the lower substitution even if the lower bound is zero.

blocks.title: Subtract the whole lower evaluation
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{1}^{3}\left(6 x - 8\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
blocks.hint: The lower evaluation is negative. Keep its sign inside brackets during the subtraction.
blocks.solution:
Use the power rule twice. Check both substitutions before doing the subtraction.

Use \(F(x)=3 x^{2} - 8 x\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(-5\) and \(3\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(8\).

sections.intro: A definite integral is a number. Evaluate the same antiderivative at both endpoints and subtract the lower evaluation from the upper one.

sections.title: What happens when limits are reversed?
sections.label: Reversed bounds

blocks.html:
Exchanging the bounds changes the sign of the integral.

\(\int_b^a f(x)\,\mathrm dx=-\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm dx.\)

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Follow the displayed order. If you choose to rewrite the bounds, carry the negative sign.

Follow the written limits. For an everywhere positive integrand, the integral from smaller to larger is positive. Going back from larger to smaller changes only the sign.

blocks.title: Your turn
blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\int_2^0(3x+1)\,\mathrm dx\).
blocks.hint: Use the written order \(F(0)-F(2)\).
blocks.solution: One antiderivative is \(F(x)=\frac32x^2+x\). The answer is \(F(0)-F(2)=0-8=-8\).

retry.feedback: This is the integral from \(0\) to \(2\). The written limits reverse that order.

blocks.title: Keep the displayed direction of integration
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{3}^{2}\left(2 x + 4\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
blocks.hint: Evaluate at the second number as written, then subtract the evaluation at the first.
blocks.solution:
The underlying integrand is positive from \(2\) to \(3\). With the limits reversed the result must be negative.

Use \(F(x)=x^{2} + 4 x\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(21\) and \(12\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(-9\).

blocks.html: The mathematically upper written limit can be numerically smaller than the lower written limit.

blocks.title: Evaluate in the direction shown by the limits
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{2}^{0}\left(6 x^{2} + 1\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
blocks.hint: The integrand is positive. Going from \(2\) back to \(0\) makes the integral negative.
blocks.solution:
Begin with the upper written limit \(0\), then subtract the value at \(2\).

Use \(F(x)=2 x^{3} + x\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(18\) and \(0\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(-18\).

sections.intro: If the displayed limits run backwards, keep their order when substituting. Swapping the two limits reverses the sign of the result.

sections.title: What if the function contains a reciprocal?
sections.label: Valid interval

blocks.html:
The ordinary evaluation uses an antiderivative on an interval where the integrand is continuous.

Before integrating a reciprocal \(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\), solve \(q(x)=0\) and compare the excluded inputs with the interval.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Check the original integrand for excluded inputs before applying the endpoint formula.

An interval lying entirely to the left of a reciprocal pole still works. The usual endpoint rule applies on that single continuous branch. A limit at the pole requires a different method.

blocks.title: Use endpoints on one continuous branch
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{-3}^{-2}\left(\frac{4}{\left(x + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
blocks.hint: The pole is at \(x=-1\), so both limits and the interval between them are on one branch.
blocks.solution:
Use power \(-2\) on the bracket, increasing it to \(-1\) and dividing by \(-1\).

Use \(F(x)=- \frac{4}{x + 1}\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(2\) and \(4\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(2\).

blocks.html: A finite answer from substituting at both ends is insufficient if the interval crosses a pole.

blocks.title: Use both powers on the positive branch
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{1}^{2}\left(2 x + \frac{4}{x^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
blocks.hint: The pole is zero. Both limits and the entire interval lie on its positive side.
blocks.solution:
The term \(2x\) contributes \(x^2\). Raising the reciprocal square's exponent to \(-1\) gives \(-\frac4x\).

Use \(F(x)=x^{2} - \frac{4}{x}\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(-3\) and \(2\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(5\).

blocks.html: Write both endpoint evaluations before rounding or simplifying.

sections.intro: Check the whole interval for a missing input, not only the endpoints. The usual endpoint calculation applies to a continuous integrand.

examples.title: Subtract the whole lower evaluation
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{-1}^{2}(2x-3)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Choose \(F(x)=x^2-3x\). Evaluate at the upper bound: \(F(2)=4-6=-2\).
Evaluate at the lower bound: \(F(-1)=1+3=4\). Parentheses help keep the sign of the substitution clear.
The integral is \(F(2)-F(-1)=-2-4=-6\). This is a signed value.

examples.title: Subtract two negative endpoint values
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{1}^{2}\left(2 x - 4\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Integrate \(2x-4\) to \(x^2-4x\). The integrand is non-positive over these limits, so the final result should be negative.
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=x^{2} - 4 x\). The written upper limit gives \(F(2)=-4\). The written lower limit gives \(F(1)=-3\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(2)-F(1)=-4-\left(-3\right)=-1\).

examples.title: Reverse the limits on a positive integrand
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_3^1(2x+1)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: The first number to substitute is the upper written limit \(1\). Use \(F(x)=x^2+x\).
Then \(F(1)=2\) and \(F(3)=12\). The integral equals \(2-12=-10\).
The integral from \(1\) to \(3\) would be \(10\). Reversing the order reverses the sign even though \(2x+1\) is positive between the endpoints.

examples.title: Reverse an interval on a negative integrand
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{2}^{1}\left(2 x - 5\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Use the limits in written order. The first is \(2\) and the second is \(1\).
The integrand is negative between \(1\) and \(2\). Reversing the usual direction changes the sign of the signed integral.
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=x^{2} - 5 x\). The written upper limit gives \(F(1)=-4\). The written lower limit gives \(F(2)=-6\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(1)-F(2)=-4-\left(-6\right)=2\).

examples.title: Check for a pole before using endpoints
examples.question: Compare \(\int_1^2\frac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm dx\) with \(\int_{-1}^2\frac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm dx\). Which can be evaluated with the ordinary endpoint rule?
solution: The first interval stays to the right of \(0\). With \(F(x)=-\frac1x\), the first integral is \(-\frac12-(-1)=\frac12\).
The second interval crosses \(0\), where the integrand has no value. No single continuous branch covers both endpoints.
Applying the same endpoint subtraction across \(0\) is invalid. This second integral has no finite value.

examples.title: Evaluate a reciprocal square on one side of its pole
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{-4}^{-2}\left(\frac{3}{\left(x + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The pole is at \(x=-1\), outside \([-4,-2]\). The integrand is positive and continuous on the whole interval.
After increasing the exponent from \(-2\) to \(-1\), dividing by \(-1\) gives \(-\frac3{x+1}\).
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=- \frac{3}{x + 1}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(-2)=3\). The written lower limit gives \(F(-4)=1\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(-2)-F(-4)=3-\left(1\right)=2\).

extraPractice.title: Evaluate a polynomial across zero
extraPractice.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{-1}^{2}\left(3 x^{2} + 1\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
extraPractice.hint: The primitive has both a cubic term and a linear term. Substitute \(-1\) into both.
extraPractice.solution:
The lower endpoint makes both terms negative, so subtracting it increases the value.

Use \(F(x)=x^{3} + x\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(-2\) and \(10\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(12\).

extraPractice.title: Evaluating endpoints with a shifted square
extraPractice.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{1}^{2}\left(18 \left(x - 1\right)^{2}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
extraPractice.hint: Keep the bracket \(x-1\) intact. The lower endpoint makes it zero.
extraPractice.solution:
The new outer exponent is three and the bracket has gradient one.

Use \(F(x)=6 \left(x - 1\right)^{3}\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(0\) and \(6\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(6\).

extraPractice.title: Use endpoint symmetry carefully
extraPractice.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{1}^{-1}\left(3 x + 2\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
extraPractice.hint: The two values of \(x^2\) agree. The linear terms have opposite signs.
extraPractice.solution:
The contributions from \(3x\) cancel on this interval, leaving the reversed contribution of the constant.

Use \(F(x)=\frac{3 x^{2}}{2} + 2 x\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(\frac{7}{2}\) and \(- \frac{1}{2}\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(-4\).

extraPractice.title: Expect a positive result from a reversed negative integral
extraPractice.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{2}^{1}\left(2 x - 10\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
extraPractice.hint: Between \(1\) and \(2\), the integrand stays negative. Reversing the direction gives a positive result.
extraPractice.solution:
Keep both negative endpoint evaluations inside the subtraction.

Use \(F(x)=x^{2} - 10 x\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(-16\) and \(-9\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(7\).

extraPractice.title: Confirm that the shifted denominator stays non-zero
extraPractice.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{0}^{1}\left(3 + \frac{2}{\left(x + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
extraPractice.hint: The only pole is at \(x=-1\). Integrate the constant and the reciprocal square separately.
extraPractice.solution:
The reciprocal-square term integrates to \(-\frac2{x+1}\).

Use \(F(x)=3 x - \frac{2}{x + 1}\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(-2\) and \(2\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(4\).

extraPractice.title: Combine a safe negative branch with reversed limits
extraPractice.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\int_{-2}^{-4}\left(1 + \frac{6}{\left(x + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
extraPractice.hint: The pole lies to the right of both limits. A positive integrand with reversed limits gives a negative value.
extraPractice.solution:
Evaluate \(x-\frac6{x+1}\) at \(-4\) first, and subtract its value at \(-2\).

Use \(F(x)=x - \frac{6}{x + 1}\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(4\) and \(-2\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(-6\).

blocks.solution:
\(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(1+x^2)^2=4x(1+x^2)\). The extra factor of two gives the required primitive.

Use \(F(x)=2 \left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}\). The endpoint values in sequence are \(2\) and \(8\). The evaluation at the written upper limit minus the evaluation at the written lower limit is \(6\).

sections.title: How can a root derivative give a related integral?

blocks.html:
A root derivative produces both a square-root denominator and the derivative of its argument.

\(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\sqrt{g(x)}=\frac{g'(x)}{2\sqrt{g(x)}}\quad(g(x)>0).\)

examples.title: Recognise the inner derivative
examples.question: Find \(\int 6x(1+x^2)^2\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: The inner expression is \(u=1+x^2\), whose derivative is \(2x\). The integrand is \(3u^2\) times this derivative.
An antiderivative has the form \(u^3+C\). On differentiating, \(3u^2\) is multiplied by \(2x\), which restores \(6x(1+x^2)^2\).
Therefore the result is \((1+x^2)^3+C\). Expansion is unnecessary.

examples.title: Find a missing scale factor in an inner derivative
examples.question: Find \(\int\left(12 x \left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{3}\right)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: The inner function is \(1+x^2\), with derivative \(2x\). The integrand has \(12x=6(2x)\).
The outer cube integrates to a fourth power divided by four. The remaining factor is \(\frac64=\frac32\).
The full family is \(\frac{3 \left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{4}}{2}+C\). Differentiate this expression to recover \(12 x \left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{3}\). Every value of \(C\) gives the same derivative.

examples.title: Recognise the derivative of a square root
examples.question: Find \(\int\frac{6x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: The derivative of \(\sqrt{x^2+4}\) is \(\frac{2x}{2\sqrt{x^2+4}}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}\).
The required numerator is six times as large, so multiply the proposed antiderivative by \(6\).
The result is \(6\sqrt{x^2+4}+C\). The radicand is positive for every real \(x\).

examples.title: Use the derivative of a square root in a definite integral
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{4}\left(\frac{2 x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The derivative of \(\sqrt{x^2+9}\) is \(\frac{2x}{2\sqrt{x^2+9}}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+9}}\).
The integrand is twice this derivative. The radicand takes the values \(9\) and \(25\) at the endpoints.
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=2 \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(4)=10\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=6\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(4)-F(0)=10-\left(6\right)=4\).

examples.title: Evaluate a reverse-chain integral with small bounds
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^1 4x(1+x^2)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Differentiate the proposed antiderivative \((1+x^2)^2\). The result is \(2(1+x^2)\cdot2x\), which matches the integrand.
Subtract \(F(1)-F(0)=3\). These are the original \(x\)-bounds because the primitive is written in \(x\).

examples.title: Recognise the derivative of a reciprocal
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{4 x}{\left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: Use the derivative \(2x\) of the inner function \(1+x^2\). The outer exponent rises to \(-1\), so the coefficient changes sign.
With the numerator \(4x=2(2x)\), the primitive is \(-2(1+x^2)^{-1}\).
An antiderivative is \(F(x)=- \frac{2}{x^{2} + 1}\). The written upper limit gives \(F(1)=-1\). The written lower limit gives \(F(0)=-2\).
Subtract the whole lower evaluation. \(F(1)-F(0)=-1-\left(-2\right)=1\).
